meta.subtitle: A cheap, improving money-center bank growing its balance sheet again, with rising returns and heavy buybacks

analystSentiment.commentary: Wells Fargo is a large U.S. money-center bank — consumer and small-business banking, commercial banking, corporate and investment banking, and wealth management — and the story this quarter is a turn in the trajectory. For years the bank could not grow its balance sheet, and it is now doing so again: on management's own account it is 'carefully deploying capital to grow', and the numbers show it, with average loans up 12% and average deposits up 10% year over year. That balance-sheet growth is flowing through to results. Second-quarter net income was $6.4 billion, or $2.00 per share — the latter up 25% as the buyback shrank the share count faster than net income grew — on revenue up 9% (net interest income up 5%, noninterest income up 13%), and the returns improved sharply: return on tangible common equity rose to 17.7% from 15.2% a year earlier, with positive operating leverage as revenue outgrew a 2% rise in expenses. The shares are inexpensive for that: at $86.12 they trade at 12.5x trailing and about 10.8x FY27E earnings — undemanding for a bank earning those returns — and the bank is returning capital hard, with roughly $7 billion of buybacks across first-half 2026 and a planned 11% dividend increase. The Street is constructive: 16 of 26 analysts rate it Buy, none Sell, with a $100.46 consensus target 16.6% above the price. We rate WFC BUY with an $88–$108 target range and a fair value just below the consensus. The discount is modest because we largely agree: the caveat is that the sharp returns come partly from a benign credit environment and a strong economy management itself flags, and a lower CET1 ratio leaves a thinner buffer than before.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Wells Fargo, a large U.S. money-center bank, serves consumers and businesses through consumer and small-business banking, commercial banking, corporate and investment banking, and wealth and investment management. FY25 produced total revenue of $83.7B, net income of $21.3B and $6.26 of diluted EPS, and the trajectory has turned up: after years in which it could not grow its balance sheet, the bank is expanding again, with second-quarter average loans up 12% and deposits up 10% year over year. The economics are those of a well-run bank at a strong point — a 17.7% return on tangible common equity in the quarter, up from 15.2% a year earlier, and positive operating leverage — and the capital story is aggressive return: FY25 buybacks of $17.5B and dividends of $5.4B, with roughly $7 billion more of repurchases across first-half 2026 and a planned dividend increase. The one figure moving the other way is the capital ratio: the CET1 ratio was 10.3% in the quarter, down from 11.1% a year earlier, as the bank deploys its buffer into growth and buybacks — still above regulatory minimums, but a thinner cushion than before. At $86.12 the market capitalizes the franchise at about $260.4B.

thesis.label: BUY
thesis.body: Wells Fargo is a cheap bank whose earnings power is inflecting up as it grows again, and the question is how much of the improvement is durable versus cyclical. The bull case is straightforward: balance-sheet growth has resumed, revenue is compounding (up 9% in the quarter), returns are rising (ROTCE at 17.7% and climbing), operating leverage is positive as expenses grow far slower than revenue, and the bank is buying back a large share of its market value every year at a low forward multiple — a combination that compounds per-share value quickly. The bear case is that a good deal of this rests on a strong economy and benign credit that management explicitly says will not last forever, and that the bank is funding the growth and the buybacks partly by drawing down its capital ratio. Our base case is that the reacceleration is real and continues at a more moderate pace, credit normalizes gradually rather than sharply, and the buyback keeps compounding EPS while the multiple stays low. We rate it BUY on that base and hold our fair value just below the Street, because the valuation is undemanding and the direction is right, tempered by the cyclicality of the returns and the shrinking capital buffer.

catalysts: Balance-sheet growth continuing — average loans up 12% and deposits up 10% — would extend the revenue and net-interest-income growth the financials section sets out.
Rising returns: return on tangible common equity climbing toward the high teens, with positive operating leverage, lifts the earnings the cheap multiple is applied to.
Aggressive capital return: roughly $7 billion of first-half buybacks at a low multiple, plus a planned 11% dividend increase, shrinks the share count and raises per-share value.
A re-rating of the multiple as the market gains confidence the improved returns are durable rather than cyclical.
risks: Credit normalization: the strong returns come with benign credit that management says reflects a strong economy, not a permanent state.
A thinner capital buffer: the CET1 ratio fell to 10.3% as capital is deployed into growth and buybacks, leaving less cushion.
Rate and cycle sensitivity: net interest income and loan growth track the rate path and the economy, both of which can turn.
Valuation depends on durability: the cheap multiple re-rates only if the market believes the higher returns last.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Wells Fargo's income statement is read on bank terms, not industrial ones: there is no gross-profit or operating-income line, and the profitability figures that matter are revenue, the efficiency of turning it into net income, and the returns on capital. The five-year revenue line runs from $79.2B in FY21 to $83.7B in FY25, roughly flat across the middle years and reaccelerating lately, and net income recovered from a $13.7B trough in FY22 to $21.3B in FY25 with diluted EPS climbing from that year's $3.27 to $6.26 — the FY22 dip is not explained in the pack, so we read the recovery rather than the cause. The latest quarter is where the inflection shows. Total revenue of $22.6 billion was up 9% year over year, with net interest income up 5% and noninterest income up 13%; net income was $6.4 billion, or $2.00 per share, up 25% as the buyback shrank the share count faster than net income grew. The quality of it is in the operating leverage: that revenue growth ran well ahead of the 2% rise in noninterest expense, so more of each incremental dollar reached the bottom line, and the provision for credit losses actually fell year over year to $914 million as charge-offs declined. The returns followed: a 15.0% return on equity and a 17.7% return on tangible common equity, both up sharply from a year earlier. Consensus looks for revenue near $88.8B in FY26E and $92.8B in FY27E, with EPS of $7.31 then $7.96 — the mid-single-digit revenue growth and buyback-driven per-share compounding the valuation is priced on.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet is where the turn is clearest and the one caution sits. Average loans grew 12% and average deposits 10% year over year — the balance-sheet expansion management describes as finally being able to grow again — and that growth is the engine behind the net-interest-income and revenue gains above. As with any bank, the familiar leverage metrics do not apply: there is no meaningful operating margin, EV/EBITDA or net-debt ratio here, and the 'total debt' line the statement carries is a slice of funding rather than the leverage story, which for a bank is regulatory capital. On that measure Wells Fargo is adequately but no longer amply capitalized: the CET1 ratio was 10.3% in the quarter, down from 11.1% a year earlier, because the bank is deploying its capital buffer into loan growth and heavy buybacks at once. Management notes it keeps 'significant buffers above regulatory minimums' and is watching the finalization of new proposed capital rules, so this is a deliberate, monitored draw-down rather than a stretch — but it does mean the cushion that absorbs a credit shock is thinner than it was, which is the counterpoint to the growth story. Total common equity supports book value, but the return figure to judge the bank on is the return on tangible common equity noted above, not a book-value multiple.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: A bank's cash-flow statement is dominated by balance-sheet movements — loans, deposits, and securities — rather than an industrial-style free cash flow, so the meaningful cash story here is capital return, and Wells Fargo's is substantial. FY25 returned $17.5B through buybacks and $5.4B through dividends, and the pace has continued: the bank repurchased about $7 billion of common stock across first-half 2026, including 37.4 million shares for $3.0 billion in the second quarter, and expects to raise the quarterly dividend 11% to $0.50 per share, subject to board approval. At that price, buying back this much stock is highly accretive to per-share value — retiring shares cheaply is one of the cleanest ways a bank compounds EPS — and it is the main reason per-share earnings outgrew net income this quarter. The discipline to watch is the interaction with the capital ratio: the same capital funding the buyback is the capital that left the CET1 ratio lower, so the buyback pace is ultimately governed by how much capital the bank generates and how much cushion it chooses to keep. Strong current capital generation supports both the growth and the return; a credit downturn would force a choice between them.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: Wells Fargo is priced as a bank the market does not yet fully trust to sustain its improvement. At $86.12 the shares trade at 12.5x trailing and about 10.8x FY27E earnings, at 3.0x sales, and at a 2.32% dividend yield — undemanding multiples for a bank now earning a 17.7% return on tangible common equity and growing. EV/EBITDA and the leverage ratios are not shown because they are not meaningful for a bank; the earnings multiple and the return on tangible common equity carry the valuation. The cheapness is the opportunity and the skepticism at once: a bank compounding EPS in the mid-to-high teens through growth and buybacks, at barely 11x forward earnings, re-rates meaningfully if the market comes to believe the improved returns are durable — and stays cheap if it does not. The Street leans that way without being euphoric: 26 analysts split Buy 16, Hold 10, Sell 0, around a $100.46 consensus target (median $102.00) that sits 16.6% above the price, inside a $90.00–$115.00 range whose low end is close to the current price. We are near the Street rather than far from it. No peer column exists in this pack, so the multiples are judged against Wells Fargo's own history.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The improvement proves durable. Balance-sheet growth continues, return on tangible common equity holds in or above the high teens, operating leverage stays positive, credit remains benign, and the buyback keeps retiring shares at a low multiple. The market re-rates the multiple upward as it gains confidence the higher returns last, and the shares reach the top of the Street's range near the $115 high target.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The reacceleration continues at a more moderate pace. Revenue grows mid-single digits, returns hold in the mid-teens rather than climbing further, credit normalizes gradually, and the buyback keeps compounding EPS while the multiple stays modest. The shares track earnings toward the consensus target as the share count falls.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The cycle turns against the bank. A slowing economy lifts credit costs from today's benign level, loan growth stalls, and lower rates or a weaker mix compress net interest income, while the thinner CET1 buffer forces the buyback to slow. Earnings fall from the current run-rate, the multiple stays low, and the shares make a fresh low, sliding below their 52-week trough.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Probability-weighting the three cases gives a fair value of about $97, roughly 13% above the price — a BUY, and one that sits just below the consensus target. We weight the Base case at 45% because a continued-but-moderating reacceleration is the most likely path for a large bank at a strong point in the cycle, and split the tails toward the bull (30%) over the bear (25%): the cheap multiple and the heavy buyback put a firmer floor under per-share value than the returns alone would, while the durability of those returns is the genuine upside. The $88–$108 target range brackets the Base outcome, and its width reflects that the swing factor is the credit and rate cycle — benign today, but cyclical. Our fair value sits close to the Street because at that low forward multiple the disagreement is narrow: the shares are cheap enough that the case rests on the durability of the improvement rather than on a demanding valuation. The discipline is to own the cheap, compounding bank on that asymmetry — a firm floor from the valuation and the buyback, with durable returns the upside.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Wells Fargo reports as a single line here, but it is a diversified bank spanning consumer and small-business banking, commercial banking, corporate and investment banking, and wealth and investment management, and the quarter's strength was broad. Total revenue of $22.6 billion rose 9%, with net interest income up 5% on the larger balance sheet and lower deposit costs and noninterest income up 13%, so both halves of a bank's revenue contributed. The diversification is the point: a bank that earns across consumer lending, commercial and corporate banking, markets, and wealth is less dependent on any one revenue driver than a monoline, which is part of why the result held up while individual lines moved at different rates. The single-line presentation understates that spread of businesses; the underlying franchise is a full-service bank with a large, low-cost deposit base as its foundation, now able to put that base to work in loan growth again.

moatFactors.name: Deposit-funding franchise
moatFactors.body: A very large deposit base — average deposits grew 10% in the quarter — gives Wells Fargo a low, sticky cost of funding that smaller banks cannot match, and lower deposit costs were a named driver of the net-interest-income growth. A large, low-cost, sticky deposit franchise is the foundational bank advantage, and it is the base from which the renewed loan growth is being funded.

moatFactors.name: Scale and diversification
moatFactors.body: The bank earns across consumer, commercial, corporate and wealth businesses at national scale, so a weak quarter in one line is usually offset by strength in another, and scale spreads the heavy fixed costs of technology, compliance and risk management across a large revenue base. That diversification is why the returns are steadier than a monoline's, and why the reacceleration showed up across both net interest income and fee revenue rather than in a single business.

moatFactors.name: Switching costs in primary banking
moatFactors.body: Consumers and businesses rarely move their primary bank — the direct-deposit, bill-pay, lending and cash-management relationships are entangled and costly to shift — so the deposit and lending relationships are durable across cycles. That stickiness is what makes the deposit base low-cost and the customer relationships long-lived, and it is the reason a large incumbent bank's franchise persists even through periods of difficulty.

moatFactors.name: Capital generation
moatFactors.body: The franchise generates capital in volume, which is what funds the loan growth and the buyback at the same time. Strong capital generation is the engine behind the whole capital-return story, and it is why the bank can draw its CET1 ratio down deliberately while still keeping buffers above the minimums — the capital-allocation section sets out how that is being spent.

businessMoat.durability: Wells Fargo's moat is wide and durable, resting on the deposit-funding franchise, national scale and diversification, and the switching costs of primary banking relationships — advantages that persisted even through the bank's period of constrained growth and are now being put back to work. The durability qualifier is not the competitive position, which is entrenched, but the cyclicality inherent in banking: returns rise and fall with credit, rates and loan demand — the cyclicality the risk section treats. So the moat is about as durable as a large bank's gets, while the level of returns it currently earns is partly cyclical. We rate the moat WIDE — the funding, scale and switching-cost advantages are real and lasting — while noting that what the improving returns and the cheap-to-rising valuation assume is not that the moat holds, which it will, but that the favorable cycle behind today's returns lasts long enough to prove them durable.

points: The core growth driver is the balance sheet finally expanding: average loans up 12% and deposits up 10% year over year, after years in which the bank could not grow it, is what drives the revenue and net-interest-income gains.
Revenue is compounding on both halves — total revenue up 9%, with net interest income up 5% on the larger balance sheet and noninterest income up 13% — so the growth is not reliant on a single line.
Operating leverage amplifies it: with revenue growing far faster than the 2% rise in expenses, incremental revenue converts to earnings at a high rate, and the returns rose accordingly.
Consensus models revenue near $88.8B in FY26E and $92.8B in FY27E with EPS of $7.31 then $7.96 — mid-single-digit revenue growth turned into faster per-share growth by the buyback.

Per-share growth is amplified by capital return: retiring a large share of the float every year at a low multiple lifts EPS well above net-income growth, as the 25% EPS gain on lower net-income growth this quarter showed.

The counter-case: this loan and deposit growth is cyclical — it leans on the strong economy and benign credit management flags — and the consensus revenue path above implies only mid-single-digit growth, a baseline rather than an acceleration, which a weaker cycle would slow.

management.leadership: Charles Scharf serves as chairman and chief executive officer, with Michael Santomassimo among the named executive officers the proxy lists. The leadership has run a multi-year effort to improve the bank's returns and efficiency, and this quarter is evidence it is working: return on tangible common equity climbed year over year, expenses grew far slower than revenue, and the balance sheet is growing again. Management's framing is notably candid on the cycle — Scharf paired the strong results with a caution that the bank is deploying capital 'through economic cycles, not just the strong environment we see today', which is the right way to read returns earned in a benign credit period. The execution record on efficiency and the return improvement is the case for the stock; the open questions are external — where credit and rates go — and how aggressively the bank draws its capital buffer to fund growth and buybacks. We weight the demonstrated operating improvement heavily.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is disciplined and shareholder-friendly, oriented around returning the bank's substantial capital generation while funding renewed growth. The bank is doing three things with its capital at once: growing the loan book (average loans up 12%), buying back stock (about $7 billion across first-half 2026, on top of $17.5B in FY25), and raising the dividend (a planned 11% increase to $0.50 a share). Buying back stock at this valuation is highly accretive, and doing it alongside loan growth is a reasonable use of capital while returns are high — but the two together are what pulled the CET1 ratio down to 10.3%, so the pace is bounded by capital generation and the buffer management chooses to keep above the minimums. The allocation is coherent for a bank confident in its returns and its capital generation; the risk in it is that a credit downturn would arrive with a thinner cushion and force the growth and the buyback to compete for a shrinking pool of capital.
management.governance: A DEF 14A proxy grounds the governance view. The board is majority-independent: every director and nominee was determined independent under the company's standards except Charles Scharf, who as a Wells Fargo employee is the sole non-independent director, so the chairman-and-CEO roles are combined in him against an otherwise fully independent board. The corporate-governance guidelines require a significant majority of independent directors and fully independent audit, governance, human-resources and risk committees. The combined chair-and-CEO structure is the one governance point some investors prefer to see split, offset here by the independent board and its committee structure. Nothing in the captured excerpt points to a governance red flag; the main thing a holder underwrites is the concentration of leadership in a CEO who has driven the turnaround.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy's ownership disclosure lists individual director and officer holdings — including Charles Scharf and Michael Santomassimo — and states plainly that none of the directors, nominees, NEOs or executive officers, individually or as a group, beneficially owns more than 1% of the outstanding common stock. As a group they beneficially owned 3,983,805 shares as of February 9, 2026. That is a modest stake relative to the float, so alignment is through equity grants rather than a control block.

idiosyncratic: Credit normalization is the primary risk. Today's returns come with benign credit — the provision for credit losses fell year over year and charge-offs declined — and management explicitly frames the environment as strong rather than permanent. A turn in the cycle would lift credit costs from a low base, and because it would arrive against a thinner capital buffer, it would bite harder than in years past.

A shrinking capital cushion. The CET1 ratio fell to 10.3% from 11.1% a year earlier as capital was deployed into growth and buybacks; it remains above minimums, but the buffer that absorbs a shock is smaller, and the pace of buybacks depends on capital generation staying strong.

Rate and net-interest-income sensitivity. Net interest income grew 5% partly on the larger balance sheet and lower deposit costs, but it is exposed to the rate path — a sharp move in rates, or a shift in deposit behavior, would change the trajectory of its principal revenue line.

Durability of the returns. The 17.7% return on tangible common equity and the operating leverage are the heart of the bull case, but a meaningful part reflects the current cycle; if the improvement proves cyclical rather than structural, the cheap multiple stays cheap.

Regulation. As a large, systemically important bank, Wells Fargo faces extensive supervision and the finalization of new capital rules management is watching, which could change how much capital it must hold and therefore how much it can lend and return.
risks.systemic: Wells Fargo is a leveraged bet on the U.S. economy and the rate cycle, as any large bank is, and the current strength of its results reflects a benign point in both. Its earnings move with credit conditions (which drive loan losses), with interest rates and the shape of the curve (which drive net interest income), with loan demand (which drives balance-sheet growth), and with the regulatory-capital regime (which governs how much it can lend and distribute). The bank has chosen this favorable moment to grow and to draw its capital buffer down, which lifts returns now but leaves it more exposed if the cycle turns — a recession, a credit shock, or a sharp rate move would each pressure results against a thinner cushion. Set against that, its scale, diversification and low-cost deposit base are exactly the attributes that let a bank come through a downturn better than smaller banks, and management's own framing shows an awareness of the cyclicality. The net picture is a franchise whose competitive position is durable and whose current returns ride the cycle the idiosyncratic risks detail.

body: We rate Wells Fargo BUY with an $88–$108 target range and a probability-weighted fair value of about $97, roughly 13% above the $86.12 price and just below the $100.46 consensus. This is a BUY on a cheap bank whose earnings power is inflecting up: after years unable to grow its balance sheet, it is expanding again — average loans up 12%, deposits up 10% — with revenue up 9%, a 17.7% return on tangible common equity up sharply from a year ago, positive operating leverage, and a large buyback retiring stock cheaply. At 12.5x trailing the market is not paying for that improvement, which is the opportunity.

The discipline is in the durability. As the risk section sets out, a meaningful part of the sharp return improvement is cyclical, and the bank is funding its growth and buybacks partly by drawing its CET1 ratio down to 10.3%, leaving a thinner buffer for a downturn. We discount for both, which is why our fair value sits modestly below the Street even as the narrow disagreement with consensus keeps it a BUY.

What would move us up: evidence that the higher returns and the balance-sheet growth are durable through a normalizing credit cycle, or a re-rating of the multiple as confidence in the returns builds. What would move us more cautious: rising credit costs against the thinner capital buffer, a stall in loan growth, or a pace of buybacks that outruns capital generation. The call is to own a cheap, improving, well-capitalized-enough bank compounding per-share value, while keeping the cyclicality of today's returns firmly in view.
